# Prepare for a Job Interview with Practice Questions from Grok

> **In short:** Give Grok your target job title (and a few details from the description) and it returns likely interview questions plus sample answers you can rehearse out loud. You'll need a Grok account (free tier works) and about 20 minutes. Grok drafts the practice set — it can't rehearse with you.

If you have an interview coming up and want to walk in better prepared, this guide walks you through building a personal rehearsal pack with Grok in one short sitting. It's written for anyone who has never asked an AI for interview help before — no prior Grok experience needed.

## Before you start
- **A Grok account.** You can use Grok on the web or inside X (the platform formerly called Twitter) if you have a Premium plan. There is a free tier with usage limits and paid plans that allow more questions. Pick whichever you already have — no need to buy anything new.
- **A web browser or the X app.** Grok works in any modern browser; the X app is fine if you go that route.
- **The job title you applied for, plus the job description if you have one.** A short paragraph is plenty.
- **About 20 minutes.** Six small prompts, plus time to read and rehearse.

## Step 1 — Open Grok and start a fresh chat
Open Grok in your browser at its website, or open the X app and look for the Grok option in the side menu (sometimes labeled "Grok" or shown with a small icon). If you're already logged in, you'll land in the chat area. Click or tap **New Chat** (or look for a **+** button, or a pencil/edit icon — apps move this around) so you begin with a clean conversation. A blank message box appears at the bottom of the screen.
💬 Example: no typing needed yet — just make sure the previous conversation, if any, is closed.
You'll know it worked when you see an empty input box with no earlier messages above it.

## Step 2 — Ask Grok for the most likely interview questions for your target role
In the empty box, type one short paragraph that names the job, the industry, and any details you want Grok to weigh (years of experience, key skills, the company name). Press Enter. Grok usually returns a numbered list — often around 8 to 12 questions — mixing technical, behavioral, and "getting to know you" prompts. If you don't see a numbered list, scroll up; sometimes the first reply appears above what you typed. If your screen looks different, look for a "Send" arrow on the right side of the box instead of pressing Enter.
💬 Example: "I'm interviewing next week for a Senior Customer Success Manager role at a mid-size SaaS company. The job involves onboarding new clients, running quarterly business reviews, and reducing churn. Give me the 10 most likely interview questions a hiring manager would ask, mixing behavioral and situational ones."
You'll know it worked when you can scroll through a numbered list of questions that feel specific to your role rather than generic.

## Step 3 — Ask for sample answers in the STAR format
Now ask Grok to draft sample answers for the behavioral questions on the list, using the STAR method — Situation, Task, Action, Result. Think of STAR as a four-part story shape: set the scene, say what you had to do, explain what you did, share the outcome. Grok will return model answers you can adapt — they won't be perfect for your life, but they show you the shape of a strong response. If your screen doesn't show structured answers, try adding the word "structured" or "with clear Situation / Task / Action / Result sections" to your prompt and ask again. Free tier accounts may run out of replies partway through — if that happens, copy what you have into a notes file and come back later.
💬 Example: "Now draft sample STAR answers for questions 1, 3, 5, and 7 from the list above. Make them 90 seconds long when spoken aloud, and use placeholder details I can replace with my own experience."
You'll know it worked when you see answers that follow a clear four-part pattern you can borrow.

## Step 4 — Ask for the awkward follow-up questions interviewers love
Real interviews rarely end after the first question — interviewers push deeper. Ask Grok to predict the follow-up probes a sharp interviewer might use, such as "What would you do differently?" or "Tell me about a time that didn't work." Grok usually returns a short list of drill-down questions for each topic. If the list feels too short, add "give me at least 5 follow-ups per main question" to the prompt. If your screen looks different, look for a way to "regenerate" the response or "try again" — most AI chat tools put that option at the bottom or top of the answer.
💬 Example: "For each of the 4 sample answers you just wrote, give me 3 likely follow-up questions an experienced interviewer would ask to push for more detail. Include at least one failure-focused follow-up."
You'll know it worked when you have a second layer of tougher questions stacked under your main answers.

## Step 5 — Add role-specific salary, culture, and scenario questions
Interviewers often slip in culture-fit or scenario questions near the end — "What would you do if a client threatened to leave?" or "Where do you see yourself in three years?" Ask Grok for those, plus common salary-range questions for your role. If you'd rather research pay on a dedicated salary site later, you can skip that part — Grok isn't a substitute for up-to-date market data, but it gives you a starting point. If the response feels vague, add "be specific to my region" or "give me a typical salary range based on recent market data" and try again.
💬 Example: "Add 5 culture-fit and scenario questions a SaaS hiring manager might ask a Senior CSM candidate, plus 3 questions about expected salary and why I want this role."
You'll know it worked when you can scan the list and recognize questions you've heard before — or ones you'd never considered.

## Step 6 — Save your best answers to a notes file for rehearsal
Highlight or copy the questions and answers you want to rehearse, paste them into a notes app, and read them out loud two or three times. Better still: practice one answer, then close the notes and try it again from memory. Grok can't rehearse with you — that's your job — but the prepared pack means you walk into the real interview having already heard your own answers in your own voice. If you want feedback on your delivery, record yourself on your phone and listen back, or ask a friend to role-play one or two questions. Plain text in any notes app works fine.
💬 Example: keep the structure simple — one line for the question, four short lines for the STAR parts.
You'll know it worked when you can deliver your top three answers out loud, in under two minutes each, without looking at your notes.

## Common mistakes
- **Asking too vaguely.** "Give me interview questions" produces generic answers. Always name the job title, the industry, and one or two specifics from the job description.
- **Trusting the sample answers as your own.** Grok's drafts are templates, not your story. Swap in your real numbers, names, and details before you rehearse — interviewers can tell when a story isn't yours.
- **Forgetting the follow-ups.** The first answer is rarely where the interview ends. If you only practice the top-level questions, the second-level probes will catch you off guard. Build at least one layer of follow-ups for every behavioral question you rehearse.

## What this means for you
- **If you're actively job-hunting:** Build a fresh Grok practice pack for each role you apply to — the questions shift a lot between, say, a Customer Success Manager and a Data Analyst, even at the same company.
- **If you hire or manage a team:** Send this workflow to anyone you're mentoring. Twenty minutes of focused practice with a personal rehearsal pack noticeably improves interview performance, and it's something they can repeat for every role.
- **If you've been out of the interview loop for a while:** Start small. One prompt, ten questions, three rehearsed answers. You don't need to master everything before your next application — just the next conversation.

## Try it now
Open Grok and send this prompt right now: "Give me 8 likely interview questions for a [your job title] role, mixing behavioral and situational questions." Read the list once, pick the three that worry you most, and draft a 60-second answer for each before you close the tab.
